meaning: An Indian word for ten million. One crore is a hundred lakh.
analogy: A crore is a hundred lakh, the way a rupee is a hundred paise.
why: Company figures in India are nearly always given in crore, so it helps to picture the size.

meaning: Money a business has borrowed and must pay back, with interest, whether it does well or not.
analogy: A home loan: the monthly payment is due even in a month when money is tight.
why: Heavy loans make a business fragile; a bad year can become a crisis.
template: {company} owed {debt} in loans in {year}.

meaning: All the money a business spends to run itself, like salaries, rent and raw material.
analogy: The household's monthly bills, from groceries to the electricity bill.
why: If costs grow faster than sales, profit shrinks even while the business grows.

meaning: The extra money a borrower pays the lender for using borrowed money.
analogy: The part of your home loan payment that is not paying back the loan itself.
why: Interest eats into profit; a company with big loans pays a lot of it every year.

meaning: The first time a company sells its shares to the public, so anyone can own a piece of it.
analogy: A family restaurant that was only ever owned by the family now lets customers buy a slice of it.
why: It is your chance to buy shares before they start trading on the stock exchange.
template: {company} is raising {issue_size} through its IPO.

meaning: An Indian word for one hundred thousand. A hundred lakh make one crore.
analogy: A small flat's down payment is often counted in lakh.
why: Small companies' figures and many prices are given in lakh.

meaning: When a business spends more than it earns in a year. The gap comes out of its savings or new money.
analogy: A month when the household spends more than it earns and dips into savings.
why: A company making losses has no profit to judge its price by, so buying it is more of a bet.

meaning: The money left over after a business pays all its costs. If costs are bigger, it is a loss instead.
analogy: What is left in the household budget at month end after rent, groceries and school fees.
why: In the long run a share is worth what the business can earn for its owners.
template: {company} kept {pat} as profit in {year}.

meaning: All the money a business takes in from selling its goods or services, before paying any costs.
analogy: Everything that goes into a kirana shop's cash box in a year, before rent, stock and salaries.
why: Growing sales show customers want more of what the company sells.
template: {company} made sales of {revenue} in {year}.

meaning: One small piece of ownership in a company. Own more pieces and you own more of it.
analogy: Ten friends chip in to open a chai stall; each friend's part is one share of the stall.
why: Buying in an IPO means buying shares, so you become a part-owner of the business.
template: At the top of the price band, one share of {company} costs {price}.

meaning: The official marketplace where shares are bought and sold on weekdays, like NSE and BSE in India.
analogy: A big sabzi mandi with strict rules, where buyers and sellers meet and prices are shown to all.
why: After the IPO your shares trade here, so you can sell them whenever the market is open.

meaning: The day it is decided who gets shares in an IPO, and how many. When demand is high, it is a lucky draw.
analogy: A housing society lottery when more families apply than there are flats.
why: Applying does not mean you will get shares; most popular IPOs give each person one bundle at most.

meaning: The time we suggest you finish applying, earlier than the exchange's evening close, because many banks and brokers stop taking applications sooner.
analogy: Getting to the station twenty minutes before the train, not as the doors close.
why: Last-minute applications often fail when banking apps are busy on the closing day.

meaning: Your offer to buy shares in an IPO, saying how many bundles you want and at what price.
analogy: Raising your hand at an auction with the price you will pay.
why: You can bid at any price in the band; bidding at the top gives you the best chance.

meaning: An account that holds your shares in electronic form, the way a bank account holds your money.
analogy: A digital locker for shares instead of paper certificates.
why: You need one to apply in an IPO; the shares you get land there.

meaning: A company's year for its accounts. In India it runs from April to March, and is named after the year it ends in.
analogy: A school year that does not start in January either.
why: All the figures in an IPO document are given by fiscal year, so you know which year you are looking at.

meaning: The total money an IPO aims to raise, at the top price, counting every share on offer.
analogy: The full price of all the flats a builder is putting up for sale in one launch.
why: Bigger issues need more buyers; small ones can be easier to fill but harder to sell later.
template: This IPO is {issue_size} in total.

meaning: The first day a company's shares start trading on the stock exchange after the IPO.
analogy: Opening day of a new shop, when you see how many customers walk in.
why: The first trading price decides whether IPO buyers are up or down on day one.

meaning: The price at which the shares first trade on listing day.
analogy: The first price at which a new model of phone resells after launch.
why: Compared with the IPO price, it shows whether early buyers made or lost money.

meaning: The smallest bundle of shares you can apply for in an IPO. You apply in whole bundles.
analogy: Eggs sold only by the tray, never one by one.
why: The cost of one bundle is the least money you need to apply.
template: One lot is {lot_size:plain} shares, costing {lot_cost} at the top price.

meaning: The main part of NSE and BSE, where bigger companies list their shares under stricter rules.
analogy: The main stage at a festival, with bigger acts and more security checks.
why: Mainboard issues face more checks than small-company issues, which lowers some risks.

meaning: The lowest and highest price for each share that a company will accept in its IPO.
analogy: A flat sold with a floor price and a ceiling price fixed before bidding starts.
why: Most people bid at the top of the band, so the upper price is what you usually pay.
template: {company}'s price band is {price_low} to {price} a share.

meaning: Getting your blocked money back when you are not given shares in an IPO.
analogy: The advance returned when the wedding hall you booked is given to someone else.
why: Your money is stuck for a few days during an IPO, even if you end up with nothing.

aliases: Securities and Exchange Board of India
meaning: India's market regulator. It writes the rules for selling shares and checks a company's IPO papers.
analogy: Like a municipal body that must approve a building plan before construction starts.
why: SEBI reviews the documents, but its approval is not a promise that the share is a good buy.

meaning: A small or medium company, listed on a separate, smaller part of the stock exchange with lighter rules.
analogy: The side stage at the festival, with smaller acts, fewer checks and a smaller crowd.
why: SME shares are fewer and less checked, so they can swing wildly and be hard to sell.

meaning: A request in your UPI app that lets your bank block the money for an IPO application until shares are given.
analogy: Like a hotel holding an amount on your card at check-in, released if you don't use it.
why: You must accept it in time, or your IPO application is not counted.

meaning: A day the stock exchange is open, Monday to Friday except market holidays. IPO timelines count only these.
analogy: Like "delivery in three business days", where weekends and holidays don't count.
why: Allotment, refund and listing dates are counted in working days, so a holiday pushes them back.

meaning: The actual cash moving in and out of a business in a period, as opposed to profit on paper.
analogy: What really landed in your bank account this month, not the salary you were promised.
why: A business can show a profit and still run out of cash if customers pay late.

meaning: The final price per share fixed after bidding closes. Small investors can tick "cut-off" to accept it, whatever it is.
analogy: Telling the auctioneer you will pay whatever the final price turns out to be.
why: Ticking it means your application isn't lost by bidding too low.

meaning: Part of a company's profit paid out in cash to its shareholders.
analogy: The landlord's share of the monthly rent from a flat they own.
why: Young IPO companies rarely pay dividends; they usually keep profit to grow.

meaning: The first draft of a company's IPO document, sent to SEBI for review. Some details may still change.
analogy: The first draft of a flat sale agreement, before both sides sign.
why: Comparing it with the final document shows what changed, such as a smaller IPO.

meaning: New shares the company creates and sells in its IPO. The money goes into the company itself.
analogy: A shop owner taking money from new partners to build a second shop.
why: Money from new shares can fund growth or pay off loans, which helps the business.
template: {fresh_issue} of this IPO is new money for {company}.

meaning: An unofficial price people quote for IPO shares before they list. Not regulated, and easy to push around.
analogy: Black-market rates for a sold-out cricket match ticket, quoted outside the stadium.
why: Treat it as gossip. It can hint at listing day mood but is often wrong.
template: An unofficial grey market premium of {gmp} a share was seen, {gmp_pct} of the price.

meaning: The bank that runs the IPO for the company, writes the papers, sets the price band and finds buyers.
analogy: The property agent who prices the flat, makes the brochure and brings in buyers.
why: They are paid by the company and want the IPO to sell, so they are not neutral.

meaning: Everything a company owes to others, such as loans and bills not yet paid.
analogy: The home loan, car loan and the unpaid bill at the kirana store.
why: If what it owes grows faster than what it owns, the company gets riskier.

meaning: How much the share price on listing day is above the IPO price. Below it is a listing loss.
analogy: A flat bought at launch price that is worth more the day it is handed over.
why: Some people apply only to sell on day one, but listing gains are never certain.
template: Recent IPOs on this board gained {recent_listing_gain} on average on their first day.

meaning: The value of a whole company at today's share price. It is the price of one share times all its shares.
analogy: The price of one flat times every flat in the building gives the building's value.
why: It tells you what the whole business costs at the IPO price, to compare with its profit and sales.
template: At the top price the whole of {company} would be valued at {market_cap}.

meaning: A pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager in shares and bonds.
analogy: A kitty party where everyone's money is handed to one trusted member to invest.
why: Mutual funds usually hold for years, so their buying an IPO is a good sign.

meaning: What the owners' part of a company is worth on paper. It is everything it owns minus everything it owes.
analogy: Your flat's value minus the home loan still unpaid on it.
why: It shows how much of the business is paid for with owners' money rather than loans.
template: {company}'s net worth was {net_worth} in {year}.

meaning: A number that tracks the prices of fifty of India's biggest listed companies, to show how the market is doing.
analogy: Like the price of a thali that tells you whether food prices overall are rising.
why: New listings tend to do better when the wider market is rising.
template: The Nifty closed at {nifty}, {nifty_gap} from its recent average.

meaning: Existing owners selling some of their shares in the IPO. The money goes to them, not to the company.
analogy: A partner leaving the shop and selling their part to someone new; the shop gets nothing.
why: If most of an IPO is owners selling, ask why they want out now.
template: {ofs} of this IPO goes to existing owners who are selling.

meaning: When buyers ask for more shares than the IPO offers, so not everyone gets what they asked for.
analogy: A wedding where more guests turn up than there are seats.
why: The more an IPO is asked for, the smaller your chance of getting shares.

meaning: Profit after every cost, interest and tax is paid. What is truly left for the owners.
analogy: Your take-home pay after tax, rent and EMIs are all paid.
why: It is the profit used to judge a company's price.
template: {company}'s profit after tax was {pat} in {year}.

meaning: Similar companies already trading on the stock exchange, used to judge whether an IPO's price is fair.
analogy: Checking what similar flats in the same area sold for before you bid on one.
why: If an IPO costs much more than its peers, you need a good reason to pay up.
template: {peer_count:plain} similar listed companies have a middle P/E of {peer_pe}.

meaning: How much of every hundred rupees of sales a business keeps as profit.
analogy: A tea seller keeping three rupees on every ten-rupee cup after milk, tea and sugar.
why: Higher margins leave more room for bad years and usually mean pricing power.
template: In {year} {company} kept {pat_margin} of its sales as profit.

meaning: The founders or main owners who control the company and are named as such in the IPO papers.
analogy: The family that started the restaurant and still runs the kitchen.
why: Founders keeping a big stake have their own money riding on the business.
template: The founders will own {promoter_post} of {company} after the IPO.

meaning: The firm that counts the applications, runs the lucky draw and sends the shares to your account.
analogy: The office that runs a housing lottery and posts the list of winners.
why: You check your allotment on its website.

meaning: An individual who applies for up to two lakh rupees of shares in an IPO.
analogy: A family buying one flat to live in, not a builder buying the whole floor.
why: A fixed part of each IPO is kept for small investors like you.
template: Small investors asked for {retail_x} the shares kept for them.

meaning: The final IPO document with the company's business, accounts, risks and the price band. Hundreds of pages long.
analogy: The full sale deed and building papers you read before buying a flat.
why: Every figure in this app comes from it, with the page number so you can check.

meaning: The chapter of the IPO papers where the company lists what could go wrong for its business.
analogy: The side effects printed on a medicine's leaflet.
why: Every risk the company itself admits to is worth reading before you buy.

meaning: The kind of business a company is in, like banking, cement or software.
analogy: Which street of the market the shop is on: cloth market, utensils market, spice market.
why: Companies are judged against others in the same line of business.

meaning: A number that tracks thirty of the biggest companies listed on BSE, like a quick health check of the market.
analogy: A thermometer for the whole stock market.
why: News often quotes it to say whether the market went up or down today.

meaning: The part of a company someone owns, given as a percentage of all its shares.
analogy: Owning two of the ten slices of a pizza is a twenty percent part of it.
why: Watch how the founders' part changes after the IPO.
template: The founders' part goes from {promoter_pre} before the IPO to {promoter_post} after it.

meaning: How many times over buyers asked for the shares on offer. Three times means demand was three times supply.
analogy: Three hundred families applying for a hundred flats.
why: Strong demand often points to a good listing day, but it is no promise.
template: Investors asked for {subscription_x} the shares on offer.

meaning: Everything a company owns that has value, like cash, machines, buildings, stock and money owed to it.
analogy: Everything a household owns: the flat, the car, jewellery and savings.
why: Compared with what it owes, it shows how solid the company's footing is.

meaning: What a company is worth, or the price the market puts on it, and whether that price is fair.
analogy: A valuer pricing a flat by its size, location and what nearby flats sold for.
why: Even a great company can be a poor buy if the price is too high.
template: At the top price {company} is valued at {market_cap}, {mcap_to_sales} its yearly sales.

meaning: Big investors who buy shares a day before the IPO opens, at the final price, to show they believe in it.
analogy: Well-known guests confirming early for a wedding, so others feel sure about coming.
why: Who the anchors are, and how long they must hold, tells you about the IPO's backing.
template: {anchor_count:plain} anchor investors put in {anchor_amount}.

meaning: An outside accountant who checks a company's accounts every year and reports if they are fair.
analogy: An inspector who checks a shop's books are honest before a loan is given.
why: An auditor quitting or objecting to the accounts is a serious warning.

meaning: A snapshot of what a company owns and owes on one day, usually the last day of March.
analogy: A list of the family's flat, savings and loans on the last day of the year.
why: It shows how much debt the company carries and how much the owners have put in.

meaning: The way most IPOs are priced. Buyers bid within a price band and the final price is set from the bids.
analogy: Selling a flat by inviting offers within a range, then fixing the price from them.
why: It is why you bid within a band rather than at one fixed price.

meaning: The steady rate a figure would have grown at each year to get from its start to its end value.
analogy: Your savings grew from one lakh to two lakh in six years: about twelve percent each year.
why: It smooths out good and bad years, so you can compare growth between companies.
template: {company}'s sales grew {revenue_cagr} a year from {start_year} to {year}.

meaning: Money spent on long-lasting things like factories, machines and buildings, rather than on running costs.
analogy: Buying a new delivery van for the shop, not paying this month's petrol.
why: IPO money spent on new capacity can grow future sales.

meaning: The money a company has in hand and in the bank, plus deposits it can use almost at once.
analogy: The cash at home plus the money in your savings account.
why: A cash cushion helps a company ride out bad times.

meaning: The record of cash coming in and going out of a company over a year, split into business, investing and borrowing.
analogy: Your bank statement, sorted into salary, spending and loans.
why: It shows whether profit actually turns into cash.

meaning: The cash the main business actually brought in during a year, after paying its running costs.
analogy: What a shopkeeper really collected in the cash box, not what customers still owe.
why: Profit that never turns into cash is a warning: customers may not be paying.
template: {company}'s business brought in {cfo} of cash in {year}.

meaning: How much of a company's sales come from just a few customers.
analogy: A tiffin service with one office as its main client: lose that office and most income goes.
why: Losing one big customer can sink sales overnight.
template: Its top customers bring in {top_customers} of its sales.

meaning: When a company creates new shares, each existing share becomes a smaller part of the company.
analogy: Cutting the same pizza into more slices: each slice gets smaller.
why: New shares raise money but spread profit over more shares.

meaning: Profit from the main business before interest, tax and the yearly cost of ageing machines are taken off.
analogy: A shop's takings minus stock, rent and salaries, before the loan EMI and taxes.
why: It shows how well the core business earns, before money matters muddy it.
template: {company}'s operating profit (EBITDA) was {ebitda} in {year}.

meaning: A small part of an IPO kept for the company's own staff, sometimes at a discount.
analogy: A builder setting aside a few flats for its own workers.
why: Staff wanting shares can be a mild sign of faith in their employer.

meaning: A company's profit after tax divided by its number of shares. The profit each share earns.
analogy: The year's profit of a shop split equally among its partners.
why: The P/E is worked out from it, so it is the base of most price comparisons.
template: {company} earned {eps} of profit per share.

meaning: Investors from outside India who buy Indian shares, such as foreign funds.
analogy: Buyers from another city who come to your town's property fair.
why: Some hold for years; others trade in and out quickly.

meaning: Money from an IPO that the company can spend however it likes, without saying how in advance.
analogy: The "miscellaneous" line in a household budget.
why: The rules cap it at a quarter of the new money; a big share is vague.
template: {gcp_share} of the new money is for general corporate purposes.

meaning: A number that shows how nervous the market expects to be over the next month. Higher means more nervous.
analogy: A weather forecast for storms in the market.
why: New listings often do worse when markets are jumpy.
template: India VIX, the market's fear gauge, stood at {vix}.

meaning: Goods and raw material a company holds that it has not yet sold.
analogy: The sacks of rice and boxes of soap sitting in a kirana shop's back room.
why: Piling up unsold goods ties up cash and may hide weak demand.

meaning: The fees a company pays to bankers, lawyers and the stock exchange to hold its IPO.
analogy: Stamp duty, the broker's fee and the lawyer's fee when you buy a flat.
why: They come out of the money raised, leaving less for the business.

meaning: A number the company itself chooses to show how its business is doing, like stores opened or orders delivered.
analogy: A cricketer's batting average, the figure everyone watches.
why: Companies pick the figures that flatter them, so read them alongside the accounts.

meaning: Court cases and legal claims a company, its founders or its managers are part of.
analogy: A property dispute that could cost the family its flat if it goes badly.
why: Cases against the company that are big next to its size can threaten it.
template: Open cases against it add up to {litigation_share} of its net worth.

meaning: A period after the IPO when certain owners, like the founders and anchors, are not allowed to sell their shares.
analogy: A fixed deposit you can't break before it matures.
why: When it ends, a flood of shares may be sold, which can push the price down.
template: Half the anchor shares can't be sold for {anchor_lockin_days:plain} days after allotment.

meaning: Whether buyers in the stock market are mostly hopeful and buying, or worried and selling.
analogy: Whether shoppers are in a festive spending mood or holding back.
why: The same IPO can list well in a happy market and badly in a gloomy one.

meaning: The middle value when numbers are lined up from smallest to largest. Half are above it, half below.
analogy: The middle child's height in a line of five siblings.
why: One very expensive peer can't drag a median up the way it drags an average.

meaning: The average of a price over the last so many days, updated every day. It smooths out daily swings.
analogy: Judging your monthly grocery bill by the last few months' average, not one month.
why: The Nifty above its recent average suggests a rising market.

meaning: The money from new shares that the company keeps after paying the costs of the IPO.
analogy: What you keep from selling your old car after the dealer's commission.
why: This is the money actually available to grow the business.

meaning: Wealthy people and firms who apply for more than two lakh rupees of shares in an IPO.
analogy: A buyer purchasing several flats at once, not one to live in.
why: Their demand can be driven by borrowed money hunting a quick listing gain.
template: Wealthy investors asked for {nii_x} the shares kept for them.

meaning: The chapter of the IPO papers that says what the company will do with the money it raises.
analogy: A loan application that says the money is for the daughter's wedding and a new roof.
why: Money for growth is a better sign than money that only repays old loans or has no clear use.

meaning: The price of one share divided by the profit per share. How many years of today's profit you pay for.
analogy: Paying ten lakh for a shop that earns one lakh a year is paying ten years of its profit.
why: A P/E far above similar companies means you are paying extra for hopes about the future.
template: At the top price you pay about {pe:plain} years of this company's current profit.

meaning: The record of a company's sales, costs and profit over a year.
analogy: The household's yearly record of income and spending.
why: It is where sales growth and margins come from.

meaning: The founders' relatives and companies linked to them, counted together with the founders as owners.
analogy: The whole joint family, not just the person whose name is on the shop.
why: Their combined stake shows how much control the founders really keep.

meaning: Big professional investors like mutual funds, banks and insurers. Usually half of a big IPO is kept for them.
analogy: Wholesale buyers who inspect the goods closely before placing a big order.
why: Their strong demand is a sign that professionals who studied the company like it.
template: Big institutions asked for {qib_x} the shares kept for them.

meaning: Past years' accounts redone with the same rules so every year can be compared fairly.
analogy: Converting old recipes to the same cup size before comparing them.
why: The figures in the IPO papers are restated, so they may differ from older annual reports.

meaning: A few months' figures, shorter than a full year, given to show the latest results.
analogy: Checking your spending for the first half of the year, not the whole year.
why: Part-year figures are not comparable with full years until scaled up.

meaning: Money a company owes its suppliers for goods it has already received.
analogy: The bill the shop owes the wholesaler, due next month.
why: Paying suppliers late can save cash for a while but strains them.

meaning: Money customers owe a company for things already sold to them but not yet paid for.
analogy: The kirana shop's "udhaar" book of customers who will pay at month end.
why: If this grows faster than sales, customers are paying more slowly, or sales are inflated.

meaning: A comparison of one year's figure with the same figure a year before.
analogy: Comparing this Diwali's sweet-shop sales with last Diwali's.
why: Big jumps from one year to the next deserve a closer look.

meaning: The part of the NII bucket for applications above ten lakh rupees.
analogy: The VIP enclosure within the VIP stand.
why: Very high demand here often comes from borrowed money betting on listing day.

meaning: How much of the information a verdict needs was actually found. Low means many figures are missing.
analogy: A doctor's diagnosis made with only half the test reports.
why: A verdict with low confidence could change once missing figures are added.

meaning: Amounts a company may have to pay if something goes against it, like a lost court case or a guarantee called in.
analogy: Standing guarantor on a friend's loan: you pay only if your friend doesn't.
why: If they are big next to net worth, a few bad outcomes could hurt badly.

meaning: Loans divided by net worth. How many rupees a company has borrowed for every rupee of owners' money.
analogy: A fifty-lakh flat with a forty-lakh loan has much more debt than one with a ten-lakh loan.
why: Above one, lenders have more riding on the business than owners do.
template: {company} owes {debt_to_equity:plain} rupees of loans for every rupee of owners' money.

meaning: Spreading the cost of a machine or building over the years it is used, as a yearly cost.
analogy: A car losing a bit of its value every year you drive it.
why: It lowers profit without using cash, which is why EBITDA leaves it out.

meaning: Operating profit as a share of sales. How much of every hundred rupees of sales the main business earns.
analogy: A tea seller's earnings per cup before paying the stall loan.
why: Comparing it with peers shows whether the business earns more or less from each sale.
template: In {year} its operating profit was {ebitda_margin} of sales.

meaning: Ownership in a company, or the owners' money in it. Net worth is the equity on paper.
analogy: The part of your flat that you truly own, after the loan.
why: Buying shares is buying equity: you share in profit and loss alike.

meaning: Our rough range of what one share could be worth, worked out from the company's profit and its peers' P/E.
analogy: What similar flats in the same building sold for, used to judge a fair bid.
why: If the IPO price is far above this range, you are paying extra for hopes.
template: Our middle estimate is {fair_base} a share, against a price of {price}.

meaning: How many times their money a selling shareholder gets back, comparing the IPO price with what they paid.
analogy: Selling a flat for three times what you paid for it.
why: A seller getting many times their money is happy to leave, whatever comes next.
template: {top_seller} sells at {top_seller_exit} the price they paid per share.

meaning: The nominal value printed on a share, often ten rupees. It has nothing to do with its market price.
analogy: The printed price on a concert ticket, which tells you nothing about what people pay for it.
why: It is only used for book-keeping; ignore it when judging the price.

meaning: The shares of a company that can actually be bought and sold on the stock exchange, not held back by insiders.
analogy: The flats in a society actually up for sale, not the ones families live in.
why: A small float can make prices swing more, and lock-in ends can suddenly add many shares.

meaning: A single serious problem that makes this app say avoid, however good everything else looks.
analogy: A cracked foundation in a flat: nice paint doesn't matter.
why: Some red flags matter more than any amount of good news.

meaning: Investors like mutual funds, insurers and pension funds who usually buy shares to hold for years.
analogy: A family buying a flat to live in, not to flip next month.
why: Anchors who hold for years are a better sign than ones who may sell the day the lock-in ends.
template: {anchor_long_only} of the anchor money came from long-term investors.

meaning: Net worth divided by the number of shares. The paper value of the business behind one share.
analogy: Your share of the flat's value after the loan, if the flat were split among family members.
why: Comparing the price with it shows how much you pay above paper value.

meaning: Loans minus cash in hand. What a company would still owe if it used all its cash to repay loans.
analogy: A ten-lakh car loan with four lakh in savings is six lakh of net debt.
why: It is added to the market cap to find what the whole business costs.

meaning: Profit after tax as a share of sales. What the owners finally keep from every hundred rupees of sales.
analogy: Your take-home share of the shop's takings.
why: A thin margin leaves little room for a bad year.
template: In {year} it kept {pat_margin} of its sales as profit after tax.

meaning: The share price divided by the net worth per share. How much more than its paper value you pay.
analogy: Paying eighty lakh for a flat the bank values at forty lakh is twice its paper value.
why: It is the usual way to judge banks and finance companies, where profit is less telling.

meaning: Investment firms that buy stakes in private companies, aiming to sell later, often in an IPO, for a profit.
analogy: An investor who buys a run-down flat, fixes it up and plans to resell it.
why: They often sell in the IPO; how much more than their cost they get tells you a lot.

meaning: The points that split numbers lined up from smallest to largest into four equal groups.
analogy: Splitting a class by marks into four groups of equal size.
why: Our low and high estimates use the peers' lower and upper quartile P/E.

meaning: How many days, on average, customers take to pay a company after buying from it.
analogy: If your tenant pays rent sixty days late, your money is stuck for sixty days.
why: Customers suddenly paying much slower can mean sales were booked too early.
template: The days customers take to pay changed by {receivable_days_change} in a year.

meaning: Firms or people linked to the founders or managers, such as relatives or companies they own.
analogy: A shop buying all its stock from the owner's brother-in-law.
why: Lots of sales to or buying from related parties can shift money away from ordinary shareholders.

meaning: Profit after tax as a share of net worth. How hard owners' money works inside the business.
analogy: A flat that earns three lakh rent on fifty lakh of your own money earns six percent.
why: A business that earns well on its owners' money can grow without borrowing much.
template: {company} earned {roe} on its owners' money.

meaning: The IPO papers' name for return on equity, profit after tax as a share of net worth.
analogy: The same as ROE, under a different name, like brinjal and baingan.
why: It is printed in the "basis for offer price" chapter, next to peers' figures.

meaning: The part of the NII bucket for applications between two and ten lakh rupees.
analogy: The front rows of the VIP stand.
why: Shares here are given by lucky draw, like the retail part.

meaning: The short code a company's shares trade under on the stock exchange.
analogy: A train's number, used instead of its full name.
why: You search for the share by this code once it lists.

meaning: The app's overall call on an IPO, worked out by fixed rules from the company's figures.
analogy: A cricket umpire's decision, made by the rule book rather than by feel.
why: It is a summary, not advice; read the reasons behind it.

meaning: The average price that existing owners paid for their shares, as printed in the IPO papers.
analogy: What your neighbour paid for their flat a year ago, compared with the price you're offered today.
why: If you pay many times what insiders paid recently, they are cashing in on you.
template: Insiders paid {waca} a share on average; you would pay {price}, {price_vs_waca} as much.

meaning: Money tied up in running the business day to day, mostly unsold stock plus money customers still owe.
analogy: The money a shopkeeper has sunk in shelves of stock and udhaar before any of it comes back.
why: When it grows faster than sales, cash gets stuck and the company may need loans.

meaning: An auditor's warning that the accounts are not entirely fair, or that it could not check something.
analogy: A building inspector signing off with "except the wiring, which I couldn't see".
why: Any such remark in an IPO's accounts deserves a close look before buying.

meaning: Free extra shares given to existing owners. The company is no bigger; it just has more, smaller shares.
analogy: Cutting each pizza slice in two: more slices, same pizza.
why: A bonus issue just before an IPO can make insiders' cost per share look tiny.

meaning: EPS worked out as if every promised option or convertible had already become a share.
analogy: Splitting the shop's profit counting partners who have been promised a share later.
why: It is a more careful profit-per-share figure when many options exist.

meaning: Market cap plus net debt. What it would cost to buy the whole business, loans included.
analogy: Buying a shop also means taking on its loan, so the true price is both together.
why: It lets you compare companies that borrow very different amounts.

meaning: A promise to staff that they can buy company shares later at a fixed, usually low, price.
analogy: A builder promising its staff flats at the old launch price in a few years.
why: Large ESOPs add new shares later, shrinking each owner's part.

meaning: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. Like the P/E, but counting loans and leaving out interest and tax.
analogy: Judging a rented-out flat's price, loan included, against its yearly rent.
why: We use it to cross-check the P/E-based estimate.

meaning: Enterprise value divided by a year's sales. Used for companies with no profit to judge.
analogy: Valuing a new restaurant by its takings, as it isn't profitable yet.
why: For loss-making companies, it replaces the P/E as the price check.

meaning: How easily you can sell a share quickly without pushing its price down.
analogy: Gold is easy to sell for cash; a plot of land in a remote village is not.
why: Small IPOs can be hard to sell in a falling market.

meaning: A firm that must keep buying and selling an SME share every day, so there is always someone to trade with.
analogy: A shop that promises to always buy back the phones it sells, at some price.
why: SME shares can be hard to sell; this makes it a little easier.

meaning: Shares sold privately to chosen investors shortly before the IPO, often at a price close to the IPO's.
analogy: Flats sold quietly to the builder's contacts just before the public launch.
why: Its price is a recent clue to what insiders think the shares are worth.

meaning: Shares the founders have given to a lender as security for a loan.
analogy: Gold jewellery given to a bank against a gold loan.
why: If the price falls, lenders may sell the pledged shares, pushing it down further.

meaning: Operating profit as a share of all the money in the business, from owners and lenders alike.
analogy: Rent from a flat bought partly with a loan, judged against its full price, not just your part.
why: Unlike ROE, it can't be pumped up by borrowing more.

meaning: How much and how fast a share's price swings up and down.
analogy: Tomato prices, which jump around far more than rice prices.
why: New listings are often very jumpy in their first months.

meaning: The assumption that a company will keep running for the next year. Doubt about it is a grave warning.
analogy: A doctor saying the patient may not make it through the year.
why: An auditor doubting a company can survive is about as bad as it gets.

meaning: Permission for the IPO's bank to sell extra shares and buy back some after listing to steady the price.
analogy: A shop keeping spare stock to calm prices if a rush of buyers comes.
why: It can support the price for a short while after listing.

meaning: What an owner originally paid for their shares, used to work out their gain on selling.
analogy: The price you paid for your flat, used to work out your gain on selling it.
why: Sellers' cost is printed in the IPO papers, so you can see their gain.

meaning: When most costs are fixed, so profit rises much faster than sales in good years and falls faster in bad ones.
analogy: A cinema's rent is the same whether the show is full or empty.
why: It explains why profit can swing far more than sales.

meaning: Shares changing hands between owners, with no money going to the company itself.
analogy: One flat owner selling to another; the builder gets nothing.
why: Recent sale prices between insiders show what they valued the company at.

meaning: When a company cuts each share into smaller ones, so each share's price falls but owners' total value stays the same.
analogy: Changing a hundred-rupee note for five twenties gives more notes but the same money.
why: Past prices must count splits and bonus shares, or a later price looks like a crash when it wasn't.

meaning: Extra checks auditors must report on, such as unpaid dues, loans to directors and fraud.
analogy: A standard checklist the inspector must tick through on every visit.
why: Remarks under it can flag unpaid taxes or loans that look odd.

meaning: How much more an investment gained than the Nifty over the same days. Below zero means it did worse.
analogy: Your mango crop grew a fifth while the village's grew a tenth, so you beat the village.
why: Any share can rise in a rising market; beating the Nifty shows the choice itself paid off.

meaning: Trying a set of rules on past cases to see how well they would have worked then.
analogy: Checking a cricket coach's tips against last season's matches before trusting them this season.
why: It shows whether a higher score really went with better results, or only looked clever.

meaning: Mistakenly using information from later when judging a past choice, which makes rules look better than they were.
analogy: Grading last year's exam guesses while holding this year's answer key.
why: A fair backtest scores each past IPO only with what was known on its closing day.

meaning: How many cases a result is based on. Fewer cases means luck can easily swing the result.
analogy: Judging a restaurant from one meal versus from twenty meals.
why: A group of five past IPOs can look great by chance; trust bigger groups more.
